content.text: An ideal transformer converts $240\,\mathrm{V}$ to $2200\,\mathrm{V}$. Which row in the table best describes the transformer?
Type of transformer: Step up; Number of turns in primary coil: 120; Number of turns in secondary coil: 1100

Type of transformer: Step down; Number of turns in primary coil: 120; Number of turns in secondary coil: 1100
Type of transformer: Step down; Number of turns in primary coil: 1100; Number of turns in secondary coil: 120
First decide what kind of transformer this is by comparing the input voltage with the output voltage, before you look at any row.

For an ideal transformer $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s$, so the coil with the greater number of turns must be the one at the greater voltage. Check each row for both the direction of the step and whether the turn counts match the voltage ratio.

The secondary voltage is greater than the primary voltage, so for an ideal transformer the number of turns in the secondary coil must be greater than in the primary: $V_p/V_s = N_p/N_s = 240/2200$, giving a $120:1100$ ratio of turns.

content.text: A planet orbits a star in an elliptical orbit as shown.

content.alt_text: Elliptical orbit diagram. A star symbol sits at the right-hand focus of the ellipse. Four points are marked on the orbit: X at the top, W at the right end nearest the star, Z at the bottom and Y at the left end furthest from the star. A 'Planet' label and arrow point to a filled dot on the upper-left part of the ellipse, with an arrow showing anticlockwise motion.

content.text: X
Y
W
Z
Use the law of ellipses and the law of equal areas to work out where along the orbit the planet is speeding up and where it is slowing down.

Do this by resolving the gravitational force at each labelled point into a component along the planet's instantaneous velocity there: a component in the direction of motion does positive work on the planet, while a component against it does negative work.
D

The star sits at the right-hand focus of the ellipse, so $W$, the end of the ellipse nearest the star, is the periapsis and $Y$, the far end, is the apoapsis. Kepler's second law fixes where the planet is fastest and slowest: it sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so it moves fastest at periapsis and slowest at apoapsis.

The arrow on the figure shows anticlockwise motion, so the planet travels in the order $W \rightarrow X \rightarrow Y \rightarrow Z \rightarrow W$. Over the half orbit from $W$ to $Y$ it is moving away from the star and slowing down; over the half orbit from $Y$ back to $W$ it is moving towards the star and speeding up.

$Z$ lies on the $Y \rightarrow W$ segment, so there the gravitational force has a component along the planet's instantaneous velocity, that component does positive work on the planet, and the planet's kinetic energy is increasing. The answer is therefore $D$, $Z$.

items: 1 mark: selects option D (Z), recognising that the planet travels anticlockwise from the apoapsis $Y$ towards the periapsis $W$, so at $Z$ the gravitational force does positive work and the planet's kinetic energy is increasing.

content.text: A satellite in a circular orbit around Earth at an altitude of $500\,\mathrm{km}$ is moved to a new circular orbit at a higher altitude of $35\,800\,\mathrm{km}$. Which statement correctly compares properties of the satellite in the higher orbit with its properties in the lower orbit?
Its period is greater, and its acceleration is the same.
Its kinetic energy is less, and its acceleration is less.
Its orbital velocity is less, and its potential energy is positive.
Its escape velocity is greater, and the centripetal force is less.
Write down the orbital relationships before judging any option: $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, $U = -GMm/r$, $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$ and $T^2 \propto r^3$.
Only the orbital radius differs between the two orbits, so every other property follows from whether that radius has increased or decreased.
B

Moving to a higher orbit increases the radius, so the orbital speed decreases ($v = \sqrt{GM/r}$) and hence the kinetic energy $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ decreases. The gravitational field strength and therefore the centripetal acceleration, $g = GM/r^{2}$, also decrease. The period increases, the potential energy becomes more negative (not positive) and the escape velocity $\sqrt{2GM/r}$ decreases, so the acceleration does change and the potential energy is not positive.

items: 1 mark: selects the row in which both the kinetic energy and the acceleration are correctly stated as decreasing in the higher orbit, using $v = \sqrt{GM/r}$, $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ and $g = GM/r^{2}$

content.text: The time of flight of the projectile is $t$. Which row in the table best describes the time to reach maximum height and the speed of the projectile at Q?

content.text: Based on the information in the diagram, which of the following statements about the two stars is true?
Star A has a lower density than Star B.
Star A has a greater rotational velocity than Star B.
Star A has a greater translational velocity than Star B.
Star A and Star B have different chemical compositions.
Treat the line positions and the line widths as two separate pieces of information. First check whether every line in one spectrum has a partner at exactly the same wavelength in the other.

If the positions match exactly, then the composition and the motion towards or away from Earth are the same, so the remaining evidence is in the widths: the wider set of lines belongs to the star whose conditions smear out the exact absorption wavelengths more.
A
Read the two spectra as two separate pieces of evidence: where the lines are, and how wide they are.

Measuring the source figures (2025 HSC Physics, assets q09_1 and q09_2), all seven absorption lines of Star A have a partner in Star B at the same wavelength, the centres agreeing to within a pixel on every line, while every line in Star B is about three times wider than its counterpart in Star A, roughly 21 units against 7. Identical positions mean the same absorbing species, so the two stars have the same chemical composition, and no relative motion along the line of sight, since a Doppler shift would displace the whole pattern towards the blue or the red and there is no such displacement in the figure.

That rules out the composition option and the translational velocity option. What remains is the broadening, which can only come from larger internal motions in Star B, either faster rotation of the surface or hotter, denser gas in which the collisions are more frequent. Either way the star with the wide lines is the star with the more extreme internal conditions, so Star A is the cooler, less dense of the two. It also follows that it is Star B, not Star A, whose rotation is the greater, which is the wrong way round for that option.
Hence the only true statement is A: Star A has a lower density than Star B.

content.text: Some material falls into the running motor, causing it to slow down. What is the subsequent ammeter reading likely to be?
Between $0$ and $0.5\,\mathrm{A}$
$0.5\,\mathrm{A}$
Greater than $0.5\,\mathrm{A}$
Treat the motor as a source of back emf in series with its internal resistance and write $V = \varepsilon_{back} + IR$.
Ask what happens to the back emf when the coil rotates more slowly, and then what must happen to the current for the supply voltage to stay fixed.

As the motor slows, the back emf generated in the rotating coil falls. The supply voltage is fixed, so the increased voltage across the motor's resistance drives a larger current: $I = (V - \varepsilon_{\mathrm{back}})/R$. Hence the ammeter reading rises above $0.5\,\mathrm{A}$.

The field of a long straight wire falls off as $B = \mu_0I/2\pi r$, so work out how the flux through the loop changes as it moves further away at constant speed.
Then use Lenz's law for the direction: on the side of the wire where the loop sits, the field of the straight wire points out of the page, and that flux is decreasing.
C

The field of the straight wire falls off as $B = \dfrac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. While the loop moves away from the wire at constant speed its distance $r$ grows steadily, so the flux through it, $\Phi = BA$, decreases, but at a decreasing rate: $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}\Phi}{\mathrm{d}t} = -\dfrac{BAv\mu_0 I}{2\pi r^{2}}$. The induced emf $|\varepsilon| = N\left|\dfrac{\Delta\Phi}{\Delta t}\right|$ is therefore non-zero for as long as the loop moves, and it decays towards zero along a curve. Rows A and B, which show a straight line falling to zero over the same interval, are wrong.

For the direction, the current $I$ in the straight wire runs downwards in the plane of the page and the loop sits to the right of the wire, so the right-hand grip rule puts the field through the loop out of the page. That flux is decreasing as the loop recedes, so Lenz's law requires the induced current to sustain it by creating a field out of the page inside the loop, which is an anticlockwise current. Rows B and D give clockwise and are therefore wrong, leaving row C: a decaying emf with an anticlockwise induced current.

content.text: The escape velocity from the surface of a planet, which has no atmosphere, is $v$. A mass is launched at $45^{\circ}$ to the planet's surface at $v$. What will be the subsequent motion of the mass?
A circular orbit around the planet
An elliptical orbit around the planet
A parabolic trajectory, returning to land with velocity $v$
A trajectory reaching zero velocity at an infinite distance
Compare the total mechanical energy of the mass at launch, $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} - GMm/r$, with zero: that decides whether it can ever return.
The launch angle changes how the velocity is split into components but not the total energy, so it cannot change the outcome.
D

The total energy of the mass is $\frac{1}{2}mv^{2} - GMm/r = 0$ when launched at exactly the escape velocity, since $v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$. The vertical component of the launch velocity is reduced to zero by gravity while the horizontal component carries the mass ever further away, so it reaches infinite distance with zero velocity, following a parabolic path and never returning.

content.text: A scientist has two unlabelled sources of radiation. One source emits alpha particles and the other emits beta particles.
Outline TWO methods that could be used to determine which source is the alpha emitter, and which source is the beta emitter.
Each method needs a difference in how the two radiations behave, so think about penetration power, ionising power, and what happens in an electric or magnetic field.
For any method, state both what you do and what you would observe, and say why that observation identifies one source as the alpha emitter.

Method 1, penetration: place a detector behind each source with a few millimetres of aluminium foil, or a sheet of paper, between the source and the detector. Alpha particles are stopped completely, so the count rate behind the foil drops to about zero, while beta particles are only slightly attenuated. The source that still gives a substantial count rate through the foil is the beta emitter.

Method 2, fields: place each source in a magnetic field (an electric field works equally well). The beta radiation is strongly deflected, and the two sources deflect in opposite directions because beta emission may be $\beta^{-}$ or $\beta^{+}$, whereas the alpha particles are much heavier and faster and are deflected only slightly. The source showing the greater deflection is the beta emitter.

Equivalently acceptable: tracking the paths in a cloud chamber, where alpha tracks are short, thick and straight while beta tracks are long, thin and curved; or comparing ionising power, since alpha particles ionise air strongly and beta particles weakly.
Pass the radiation from each source through a thin material to a detector. Observe any changes in counts. The beta source count will be reduced by an amount less than the alpha source count.
Pass each type of radiation through a magnetic field and observe any differences in deflection, and observe deflection in opposite directions.
Answers could include: magnetic field, electric field, cloud chamber.

2 marks: outlines a method that could be used to distinguish the sources OR identifies TWO methods that could be used to identify each source

content.text: Describe the energy transformations that take place in the transformers, and in the transmission line.

Trace the energy in three steps for a transformer: electrical in the primary coil, magnetic in the soft-iron core, electrical out of the secondary coil. At each step ask where some of that energy is leaking away as heat rather than being transferred on.

Contrast the two situations. A transformer is a stationary piece of equipment, so only its internal inefficiencies matter; the transmission line is a conductor carrying current over a long distance, so $P_{\text{loss}} = I^{2}R$ is dissipated continuously along the whole route.

In both transformers energy is transferred by electromagnetic induction (electrical $\rightarrow$ magnetic in the core $\rightarrow$ electrical in the secondary coil), but some electrical energy is dissipated as heat because of resistive heating in the windings, eddy currents and hysteresis losses in the core, and magnetostriction, so the energy out of each transformer is less than the energy in. In the transmission line the current flows through wires of non-zero resistance, so electrical energy is continuously dissipated as heat along the line, and the energy delivered to the house is less than the energy leaving transformer A.

The energy output of both transformer A and transformer B is less than the energy input. These transformers produce heat energy in their cores due to resistive losses, magnetic effects and mechanical vibrations.
In the transmission line, heat energy is produced due to the resistance of the wires.

content.text: Using the particle model of light, explain the features shown in the experimental results.

Name the model first: light is delivered in discrete packets, and the energy of each packet is set by its frequency. Then work out what has to happen to a single packet before it can release an electron from the metal surface.

For the trend, follow one photon: as the frequency of the light rises, compare the energy each electron receives with the energy it needs just to escape, and then link that surplus energy to the voltage that has to be applied to stop the electrons.

Light consists of discrete packets of energy (photons) with energy $E = hf$. Below the threshold frequency photons cannot eject electrons; above it the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons is $KE_{\max} = hf - \phi$, so increasing the frequency increases the stopping voltage linearly.

The photon model of light explains the trend by stating that light consists of discrete packets of energy called photons. The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency ($E = hf$). When photons strike the metal, they transfer energy to electrons. If the photon energy exceeds the work function of the metal, the threshold frequency is exceeded and electrons are ejected with kinetic energy proportional to the excess energy ($KE = hf - \phi$).

As the frequency of light increases, the photon energy increases, resulting in higher kinetic energy for the ejected electrons. This is observed as a higher stopping voltage, which is required to halt the more energetic electrons.

content.text: Two things have changed: the rotational speed and the direction of rotation. Take them one at a time instead of describing the new curve in a single step.

A change in rotational speed acts on both axes at once. Check what happens to the time for one complete cycle, and check separately what happens to the size of the peak voltage, because the peak emf depends on how quickly the flux is changing and not only on the period.

Finally ask what the voltage is doing at the instant the graph starts. The coil is at the same starting position as before, so look at how quickly the flux is changing there - fastest or not at all - and remember that reversing the rotation swaps the sign of the voltage.

A sinusoid with twice the amplitude of the printed curve and half its period, so four complete cycles fit between $0$ and $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ (period $0.05\,\mathrm{s}$). At $t = 0$ it starts at a trough — the greatest magnitude but negative — because the rotation has been reversed while the flux is changing fastest.

Two things change at once and each affects the sketch separately. Doubling the rotational rate from $10$ to $20$ revolutions per second doubles $\omega = 2\pi f$, so the period halves from $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ to $0.05\,\mathrm{s}$ and four complete cycles fit into the $0.2\,\mathrm{s}$ shown. Because $\varepsilon_{max} = NBA\omega$, the same doubling also doubles the peak voltage, so the new curve has twice the amplitude of the printed curve.

Reversing the direction of rotation leaves the magnitude of the emf unchanged at every instant but flips its sign, so the new curve is the printed curve turned upside down. In the starting position the flux through the coil is greatest and changing fastest, so the emf is at its greatest magnitude at $t = 0$, not zero — the printed 10 revolutions per second curve begins at a crest, so the new one begins at a trough.

content.text: What minimum speed is required for the rider to land on the second ramp?

Both ramps are $2\,\mathrm{m}$ high and inclined at the same angle, so the rider leaves the first ramp and lands on the second at the same height. The vertical displacement over the flight is therefore zero — the $2\,\mathrm{m}$ height is not used in the calculation.

Write the two independent equations $16 = u\cos\theta\,t$ and $0 = u\sin\theta\,t - \tfrac{1}{2}gt^{2}$ and eliminate $t$. Watch the factor of $\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the vertical equation, and note that $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ brings a further factor of 2 with it.
$u = 15.6\,\mathrm{m/s}$

The rider leaves the top of the first ramp and lands on the second ramp. Both ramps are $2\,\mathrm{m}$ high, so take-off and landing are at the same height and the net vertical displacement over the flight is zero.
Horizontally $s_x = u\cos\theta\,t$, so $t = s_x/(u\cos\theta)$.
Vertically $0 = u\sin\theta\,t + \tfrac{1}{2}a_y t^{2}$, so $u = -2a_y t/\sin\theta$.

content.text: Compare the speed of the mass at point A to that at point B. Support your answer using appropriate mathematical relationships.

Use the diagram to fix the height of each point before writing any equation. A is level with the centre of the circle and B is at the top, so the two are separated in height by exactly $r$, whatever datum you choose.

Set the total mechanical energy at A equal to that at B, writing the kinetic and gravitational potential energy at each point. Keep the factor of $\frac{1}{2}$ in the kinetic energy term carefully: the ratio of the kinetic energies is not the ratio of the speeds, so convert through $KE = \frac{1}{2}mv^{2}$ before quoting a speed ratio.
$v_A = \sqrt{1.5}\,v_B$, i.e. the speed at A is about 1.22 times the speed at B, so the speed at A is greater.
The speed of the mass at point A will be greater than $v$ from part (a). Total mechanical energy $= E_k + GPE$.
At point B: total mechanical energy $=\frac{1}{2} \times m \times gr + mg(2r) =$ total mechanical energy at A.
At A the gravitational potential energy is $mgr$ and thus $\frac{1}{2}m \times gr + 2mgr = mgr + E_{kA}$.
Simplifying gives $E_{kA} = \frac{3}{2}mgr$, so $v_A = \sqrt{1.5}\,v_B$.

content.text: Experiments have been carried out by scientists to investigate cathode rays.
Assess the contribution of the results of these experiments in developing an understanding of the existence and properties of electrons.

Break the experimental record up into the specific results that were obtained, and match each to the property it established: deflection in an electric field, deflection in a magnetic field, behaviour with different electrode materials, absorption in thin metal foils, and the ratio of electric to magnetic field needed to cancel the deflection.

Do not stop at naming a result. A result only earns the mark when you state what it changed in our understanding — the existence of the electron (a constituent of every atom) or one of its properties (negative charge, finite mass, a measured $q/m$).

The results were essential, because together they converted an unexplained 'cathode radiation' into the electron, a universal constituent of matter with known properties. Cathode rays were shown to be deflected by both electric and magnetic fields in the direction expected for negatively charged particles, and since electromagnetic waves are not deflected by a field this proved the rays were particles. Using electrodes made of different materials gave the same deflection, showing the rays did not depend on their source and that they came from the atoms themselves. Rays were absorbed by thin metal foils, showing they had mass, and were stopped by thin sheets of metal. Finally, balancing the electric and magnetic deflections and measuring the curvature of the beam in a magnetic field gave a charge-to-mass ratio of about $1.8\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{C\,kg^{-1}}$, fixing the mass of the electron at about $9.1\times10^{-31}\,\mathrm{kg}$ and leading to the nuclear model of the atom.
Experimental results and their interpretation have played an essential role in developing and understanding of both the existence and properties of electrons.

It was demonstrated that cathode rays could be deflected by an electric field in a manner consistent with negatively charged particles. This experiment also allowed the deduction that the cathode rays were not electromagnetic waves because the latter would not be deflected by an electric field.
The combined effect of changing the magnitudes of electric and magnetic fields through which the electrons passed was measured and from this the charge-to-mass ratio of the electron was calculated.
Answers could include:

items: By using electrodes made of different materials, Thomson was able to deduce that the cathode rays' properties were independent of the source of the electrons and hence that they were a constituent of atoms themselves rather than being a product of the cathode ray.
Cathode rays were passed through thin metal foils and the analysis of this behaviour allowed scientists (Lenard/Hertz) to deduce that the electrons had mass.

Crookes' observation that cathode rays travelled in straight lines and cast sharp shadows from which he deduced that the rays were particles and not waves (which would have shown diffraction effects).

content.text: Analyse the consequences of the theory of special relativity in relation to length, time and motion. Support your answer with reference to experimental evidence.

State the two postulates first — the speed of light in vacuum is the same value for all inertial observers, and the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames — then ask, for length, for time and for motion, what two such observers would disagree about and by what factor their measurements differ.

For the evidence, pick observations that were actually made on Earth: the flux of muons detected at ground level compared with their known half-life and production altitude, the energy that must be supplied to protons as their speed approaches $c$, and the round-trip light travel time measured by interferometers. For each, ask exactly which consequence it demonstrates.

items: Length: lengths measured along the direction of relative motion are length-contracted, $L = L_{0}/\gamma$, so a moving object is shorter for an observer who sees it moving but unchanged in length in its own rest frame.
Time: intervals measured by a moving clock are time-dilated, $\Delta t = \gamma\Delta t_{0}$, so a moving clock runs slow and a moving process takes longer.

Motion: the momentum of a massive object is $p = \gamma mv$, so increasingly large energy must be supplied as $v$ approaches $c$ and no massive object can reach or exceed the speed of light; with $E = mc^{2}$ mass and energy are equivalent, and massless particles travel at $c$ while massive ones cannot.

Experimental evidence: muons produced in the upper atmosphere should decay before reaching the ground, yet far more reach it than half-life alone predicts, because from Earth's frame their lifetime is dilated and from the muon's frame the atmosphere's depth is length-contracted; particle accelerators show the energy needed per unit increase of speed rising steeply as $v \to c$; and Michelson-Morley-type interferometry finds no change in round-trip light time with orientation, as special relativity requires.

content.text: The two postulates of special relativity are: the speed of light in a vacuum is an absolute constant, and all inertial frames of reference are equivalent.

The consequences of these postulates are time dilation, length contraction and relativistic momentum dilation. Time dilation means that the measured time between events increases as the speed of an observer increases. Length contraction means that the length of an object decreases as the speed of an observer increases, and relativistic momentum dilation means that objects (with mass) cannot travel at $c$ as it takes increasing amounts of energy to accelerate objects as they approach the speed of light.

Length contraction and time dilation can both be seen in observations of muons at Earth's surface. The short half-life of muons suggests that there should be very few of them that arrive at Earth's surface from their point of origin high in Earth's atmosphere, but the muon flux is greater than suggested by half-life and distance travelled alone. However, when the distance travelled is considered from the muon's frame of reference, it is length-contracted, giving an effective shorter distance for them to travel. From the perspective of an observer on Earth's surface, the time taken for them to decay is dilated, giving an effective greater amount of time for them to travel before decaying.

The effects of relativistic momentum can be seen in particle accelerators in terms of the increasing amounts of energy required to accelerate the particles as they approach the speed of light, even though the objects are much more massive than they are.

content.text: Analyse the role of experimental evidence and theoretical ideas in developing the Standard Model of matter.

Do not write two separate lists. Present the development as a repeating cycle: a theoretical idea was proposed, an experiment was designed to test it, the result either confirmed or forced a revision of the idea, and that result then made the next theoretical step possible.

Include evidence from more than one scale of apparatus — an early, inexpensive experiment such as a cloud-chamber track, and a modern particle accelerator capable of resolving distances of $10^{-18}\,\mathrm{m}$ — so that the argument shows why both theory and experiment were indispensable rather than either being sufficient alone.

Both were required and each drove the other in a repeating theory–experiment cycle. Theory came first: the quark model, Dirac's prediction of antimatter, the electroweak unification of the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces, and the Higgs mechanism were each proposed before the measurements that tested them. Experiments then supplied the resolution that theory alone could not: cloud-chamber tracks produced the positron, confirming the prediction of antimatter; deep inelastic scattering experiments showed that protons and neutrons have internal structure, verifying quarks; detection of the $W$ and $Z$ bosons confirmed the electroweak theory; and the Higgs boson was found decades after it was first proposed as necessary to explain the mass of particles. Each confirmation legitimised and sharpened the model, allowing further predictions to be made, so the Standard Model of matter is the outcome of an ongoing interplay rather than of either experiment or theory alone.
Experiments and theoretical ideas have both been critical in the development of the Standard Model of matter.

Particle accelerators have been used to verify key ideas about fundamental particles and the structure of matter. Particle accelerators allow small wavelength 'matter probes' at high energies, giving high resolution for probing the structure of matter.
Examples of particle accelerator use in the development of the Standard Model include:

items: Verification of the electroweak theory, which says that the electromagnetic and weak nuclear forces are a result of the same interaction.
The discovery of a Higgs Boson, many decades after it was first proposed as necessary in explaining the mass of particles.
Verification of the existence of quarks by showing the protons and neutrons have internal structure.

content.text: Earlier experiments used simpler equipment such as the cloud chamber which was used to discover antimatter following its earlier theoretical prediction.
Many experiments have verified earlier theoretical ideas, and these confirmations have then in turn allowed the proposal of further ideas, which have in turn later been verified by experiments.

content.text: A method to determine the speed of light using this model is described below. When Earth was at position P, the orbital period of Io was measured, and the time that Io was at position R was recorded.

Six months later, Io had orbited Jupiter $10^{3}$ times, and Earth had reached position Q. The orbital period of Io was used to predict when it would be at position R. Assume that Jupiter has not moved significantly in its orbit around the Sun.
The time for Io to reach position R was measured to be $1.000 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{s}$ later than predicted, due to the time it takes light to cross the diameter of Earth's orbit from P to Q.
Part (a) turns on identifying the distance the light actually travels. Earth moves from P to Q, which are on opposite sides of its orbit, so the light crosses the whole orbit rather than the radius.

Part (b): the measurement in (a) is a distance divided by a time, so ask separately what an elliptical orbit does to the distance and what happens to the result. A circle has one radius; an ellipse has a short axis and a long axis, and the light could be taken to travel along either.

content.text: Use the measurements provided in the model to calculate the speed of light.

The light travels from P to Q, which are diametrically opposite on Earth's orbit, so the distance is the diameter of the orbit, not the radius. Convert the radius from kilometres into metres and double it.

The measured delay is the time the light takes to make that crossing, so divide the distance by that time. The number of Io orbits is not needed - it only explains how accurately the arrival time at R can be predicted.

items: 1 mark: sets up the correct relationship and substitutes the given values: $d = 2 \times 1.471 \times 10^{11} = 2.942 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$
1 mark: correct final answer, $2.942 \times 10^{8}\,\mathrm{m/s}$, with correct units

content.text: Consider a modification to this model in which the Earth's orbit is elliptical.
Explain how this modification will affect the determination of the speed of light.

Hold the delay fixed and ask what an elliptical orbit does to the distance the light has to cross. A circle has only one radius, whereas an ellipse has a short axis and a long axis, and the two give different crossing distances.

Because the calculation is a distance divided by a time, decide separately for each axis which way the calculated speed moves, and be ready to say why. You do not need a new value for the time in order to argue this.
Using the long axis of the ellipse increases the calculated value of the speed of light; using the short axis decreases it.

If light travels along the long axis of the ellipse, then the distance travelled by the light across Earth's orbit is greater than $2.942 \times 10^{11}\,\mathrm{m}$. The effect of this would be to increase the calculated speed of light.
Answers could include a reduced speed of light due to measurement of the distance along the short axis of the ellipse.

content.text: A hollow copper pipe is placed upright on an electronic balance, which shows a reading of $300\,\mathrm{g}$. A $50\,\mathrm{g}$ magnet is suspended inside the pipe and subsequently released.

content.alt_text: Diagram of the apparatus: a hollow 'Copper pipe' standing vertically on an 'Electronic balance' whose display reads 300 g. A 'Magnet (50 g)' is shown inside the upper part of the pipe and also drawn separately above, with an arrow indicating the magnet being lowered into the pipe.

content.text: It was observed that the readings on the balance began to increase after the magnet began to fall, and that the reading reached a constant maximum of $350\,\mathrm{g}$ before the magnet reached the bottom of the tube.
Explain these observations.

Split the motion of the magnet into two phases and ask what is changing in each: while the magnet is speeding up, the rate of change of magnetic flux through the copper is changing; once the magnet is at constant speed, the flux through the wall of the pipe is no longer changing.

Remember that the force the magnet exerts on the pipe and the force the pipe exerts on the magnet are a third-law pair, and that the balance reads the total downward force on the pipe plus the pipe's own weight.

As the magnet accelerates, the rate of change of magnetic flux through the copper wall increases, so larger eddy currents are induced in the pipe. By Lenz's law these produce an upward magnetic force on the magnet that grows as it speeds up, and by Newton's third law an equal and opposite downward force on the pipe, so the balance reading rises. Once the magnet reaches terminal speed the flux change rate is constant, the upward induced force is constant, and it opposes the magnet's weight; the reading stops rising. At that point the induced force balances gravity, so the force the magnet exerts on the pipe equals the magnet's own weight, and the maximum reading is $300\,\mathrm{g} + 50\,\mathrm{g} = 350\,\mathrm{g}$ before the magnet reaches the bottom.
The reading on the scale has two phases.

items: The magnet accelerates to a maximum speed. This results in an increasing change in magnetic flux causing the creation of an increasing electromagnetic force that opposes the constant gravitational force acting on the magnet. The force on the magnet due to this interaction produces an equal and opposite force on the pipe, which results in an increase in the downward force on the scale.

The magnet reaches a constant speed when the upward electromagnetic force is equal and opposite to the weight force of the magnet. The force of the magnet on the pipe will be equal to the weight of the magnet. The reading on the scale will then be the weight of the pipe and the magnet, shown in grams.

content.text: A satellite with velocity $v$, is in a geostationary orbit as shown in Figure 1.

content.alt_text: Figure 1: the Earth drawn as a grey circle with a centre point, and a satellite shown as a filled dot on a circular orbit to the lower right of the Earth, with a dashed line from the Earth's centre to the satellite and a right-angle marker showing the orbit is tangential. A velocity arrow v points away from the Earth along the tangent at the satellite.

Figure 2: the Earth drawn as a grey circle with a centre point, and an explosion point Y on the orbit to the right of the Earth. Two pieces leave Y: piece m_a moving vertically away with a velocity arrow labelled 2v, and piece m_b at Y itself. A right-angle marker shows the velocity is perpendicular to the radius at Y.

content.text: At point Y, the satellite explodes and splits into two pieces $m_a$ and $m_b$, of identical mass. As a result of the explosion, the velocity of one piece, $m_a$, changes from $v$ to $2v$ as shown in Figure 2.
Analyse the subsequent motion of BOTH $m_a$ and $m_b$ after the explosion. Include reference to relevant conservation laws and formulae in your answer.

Begin with momentum, not with energy. The explosion is an internal force, so it is the momentum changes of the two pieces that are equal and opposite; because the pieces have identical mass, their velocity changes are equal in magnitude. Work out what that does to the velocity of $m_b$ when $m_a$'s doubles.

Then treat each piece on its own. For $m_a$ compare the post-explosion speed with the escape velocity for that radius, $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$; for $m_b$ remember that zero velocity does not mean zero acceleration in a gravitational field, and that the acceleration depends on the distance from the Earth's centre.

Momentum: the explosion is an internal force, so by conservation of momentum the momentum changes are equal and opposite, and because the pieces have equal mass their velocity changes are equal and opposite. $m_a$ increases by $v$, so $m_b$ loses $v$ and has zero velocity relative to the Earth at that instant.

$m_a$: its new speed is $2v = 2\sqrt{GM/r} = \sqrt{4GM/r}$, which exceeds the escape velocity $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$. It therefore leaves the Earth system on an unbound hyperbolic path, moving away with increasing speed, its total energy staying positive and its gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy both changing as the sum stays constant.

$m_b$: with zero initial speed it falls radially toward the centre of the Earth. Its initial acceleration is less than $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ because it is above the Earth's surface, and the acceleration increases as $r$ decreases, so it speeds up at an increasing rate until it reaches the atmosphere. Its kinetic energy increases as its gravitational potential energy becomes more negative, with the total remaining constant.
By the law of conservation of momentum, the momentum changes of $m_a$ and $m_b$ resulting from the force produced by the explosion must be equal but opposite.

Since they are of equal mass, the velocity change of both pieces must be the same, but in opposite directions. Since the velocity of $m_a$ increases by $v$ in the direction in which it was travelling, the velocity of $m_b$ is also $v$, but in the opposite direction to which it was travelling.
Hence, relative to the Earth, the velocity of $m_b$ must become zero at that instant.

The orbital velocity of the satellite prior to the explosion is given by $v_{orb}$. Hence the instantaneous velocity of $m_a$ as a result of the explosion is double the orbital velocity before the explosion, because $2v = 2v_{orb} > v_{esc} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$. The velocity of $m_a$ after the explosion is greater than the escape velocity.

After the explosion, the piece $m_a$ will continue to travel away from Earth at a decreasing velocity; however, because its initial velocity exceeds the escape velocity from the explosion point, it will never stop or return to Earth. Its total energy (kinetic + potential) remains constant and will always be positive.

Consequently, $m_b$ will begin to accelerate, from an initial velocity of zero, towards the centre of Earth. Its acceleration is initially less than $9.8\,\mathrm{m/s^{2}}$ because it is not at Earth's surface. As the force due to gravity on $m_b$ increases, its acceleration increases and so its velocity towards the centre of Earth increases at an increasing rate until it reaches Earth's atmosphere.

Consistent with the law of conservation of energy, until $m_b$ reaches Earth's atmosphere, the sum of its kinetic and potential energy must remain constant and equal to its initial potential energy at the instant after the explosion.
